messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Editor
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Female Presence: Being alone with women, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rohan Patel was 26, newly married, and working long hours as an editor when he was stopped by police one winter night driving home from the office. He had been alone, tired, and still carrying pages marked up in red on the passenger seat. What began as a traffic stop escalated into a humiliating and frightening encounter he still struggled to describe in a straight line. He remembered being ordered out into the cold, his hands positioned against the hood of the car while an officer searched him and another stood nearby. A woman officer had moved in and out of his field of vision during parts of the stop, close enough that he became acutely aware of her presence while feeling trapped and exposed. The metal of the car was freezing through his clothes, his arms were fixed awkwardly, and he could smell the mix of exhaust, wet pavement, and the officer’s latex gloves. He was not physically injured, but what stayed with him was the sense of being pinned in place, watched, and powerless, followed by a crushing grief that would hit him later whenever he tried to think about it.

In the weeks afterward, Rohan did not simply remember the stop; he seemed to drop back into it. At times, when the memory came, his body would tighten into the same strained position, shoulders braced and arms subtly held as if against the hood again. If he let himself picture that night, he could catch the smell of exhaust and cold rubber so vividly that it felt less like recollection than return, and with it came an overwhelming grief that was out of proportion to what others around him seemed to expect. That grief was tangled with what he had come to believe about himself. He was certain that the fact he still reacted this strongly meant he was a lousy coper, and the more he told himself that nothing good could happen to him anymore and that life no longer felt meaningful, the more the memory arrived saturated with loss, as if his mind kept proving his bleak conclusions true.

His work began to expose him to the problem in small, daily ways. The office was heavily air-conditioned, and when a draft hit the back of his arms in a particular way, he would suddenly feel the cold of the car hood on his skin. In those moments he would go faintly unreal, then notice that detached feeling itself and become alarmed, because the beginning of unreality had become one of the things he feared most. If he was assigned to meet alone with a female author or publicist in a conference room, he would tense before she even sat down. He had come to see these reactions as evidence of weakness; if being in a cold office, or in a room with a woman, or even feeling a little detached could throw him so badly, to him that confirmed he was not handling life like other people did. Those judgments deepened his hopelessness and made the world feel narrower and more dangerous.

Over time, the same bleak beliefs sharpened the very things that set him off. Because he was so preoccupied with the idea that he was damaged and that nothing ahead could be good, he scanned himself constantly for signs of coming apart. A flicker of detachment no longer passed unnoticed; he caught it immediately and braced for it. He became more sensitive to cold on his skin, changing the thermostat repeatedly at work and at home. Being alone with women grew loaded in his mind, not because of anything they did, but because he feared what their presence stirred in him and what that reaction said about him. His wife noticed that he made excuses to keep meetings brief or leave doors open, and he felt ashamed, reading even that pattern as further proof that he was failing at ordinary life.

The memories also seemed to make the triggers stronger in their own right. After a vivid recollection, especially one in which he could smell the roadside air and felt his body lock into that old position, the next brush of office cold or the next moment of feeling unreal seemed enough to pull him toward the edge again. The event had taught his body these cues too well. Each time that happened, he was left grieving not only the stop itself but the person he felt he had been before it, and that grief fed the conviction that his life had lost its meaning. He withdrew from his wife emotionally, saying little when she asked what was wrong because he did not know how to explain why such specific sensations had become so potent.

By the time he sought help, Rohan was still going to work but arranging his days around what he might encounter. He dreaded one-on-one editorial meetings with women, monitored the temperature of every room, and feared the first hint of unreality in his own mind. What finally brought him in was the sense that his world was shrinking and that he was becoming someone defined by this one night. He was most afraid that nothing good was ahead and that his reactions meant he would never feel like himself again, but part of him still hoped that if he could understand why these moments carried such force, his life might begin to feel meaningful again.
